name: Acetabular labral tear
populations: women with hip dysplasia or hypermobility
athletes in pivoting, kicking and end-range sports
summary: Detachment or splitting of the fibrocartilaginous rim of the hip socket, usually anterosuperior, causing groin pain and clicking. Often secondary to FAI morphology or dysplasia and common without symptoms.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: At least 3 months of exercise-based care; 4–9 months after arthroscopic repair

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: FADIR: high sensitivity, poor specificity; a negative test helps rule out intra-articular pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: 3 T MRI or MR arthrography (Sn ≈0.80–0.89, Sp ≈0.69–0.77)

keyFacts.label: Site
keyFacts.value: Anterosuperior quadrant in about three-quarters of tears

keyFacts.label: Caution
keyFacts.value: Labral tears are seen on MRI in about half of people without hip pain

keyFacts.label: Diagnostic delay
keyFacts.value: Mean 21 months from symptom onset in one surgical series

overview:
The acetabular labrum is a ring of fibrocartilage that deepens the hip socket, seals the joint and helps pressurise synovial fluid so the cartilage is protected under load [r2,r3]. Tears usually occur in the anterosuperior labrum, either as a detachment at the chondrolabral junction or as cleavage planes within its substance [r2]. In the International Hip-related Pain Research Network classification, symptomatic labral pathology without distinct bony morphology is one of three main causes of hip-related pain in young and middle-aged adults. Incidental labral tears on imaging must not be confused with this clinical condition [r1].

Most tears are secondary to abnormal hip morphology (FAI or dysplasia), repetitive end-range loading or, less often, a single twisting or traumatic event [r5,r7]. Labral tears are present on MRI in a similar proportion of people with and without pain [r4], so diagnosis rests on the clinical picture. First-line care is education, load modification and progressive exercise for at least 3 months; arthroscopic repair or debridement is considered for persistent symptoms [r11].

epidemiology.text: A meta-analysis found labral tears on MRI, MRA or CT in 62% (95% CI 47–75%) of symptomatic and 54% (95% CI 41–66%) of asymptomatic individuals, highlighting a weak link between imaging and pain [r4]. In cadaveric hips of older adults, 96% had labral tears, 74% of them in the anterosuperior quadrant [r2]. Labral tears accompany 78.8% of dysplastic hips and 93.8% of hips with FAI in surgical series [r7]. In a series of arthroscopically confirmed tears, 71% of patients were female, mean age was 38 years, onset was insidious in 61% and associated with low-energy injury in 30%, and the mean time to diagnosis was 21 months [r5].

intrinsic: Generalised joint hypermobility and capsular laxity
Reduced gluteal or iliopsoas force contribution, which increases anterior hip joint force (modifiable) [r8]
Female sex and increasing age (degenerative tears) [r2,r5]
extrinsic: Sports with repeated pivoting, kicking or end-range hip flexion and rotation
Activities that load the hip in end-range extension and external rotation (dance, sprinting, golf follow-through) [r8]
A single twisting fall, slip into the splits, or high-energy trauma such as hip subluxation [r5]

mechanism.summary: Most labral tears result from repetitive loading of the anterosuperior rim: in FAI the femoral head–neck junction shears or crushes the labrum in flexion and internal rotation; in dysplasia the labrum is overloaded as the femoral head translates toward the shallow rim [r7]. An acute tear typically occurs during a forceful twist or pivot on a loaded, flexed hip, a slip into hyperabduction, or end-range hip extension with external rotation, which increases anterior joint force [r8].
sequence: The athlete plants the right foot and pivots, so the pelvis and trunk rotate over a fixed, flexed and loaded femur.
Axial load plus rotation drives the femoral head against the anterosuperior acetabular rim.
Shear concentrates at the chondrolabral transition zone, where the labrum joins the articular cartilage [r2].
The labrum detaches from the cartilage (or splits within its substance), and the joint seal is breached [r2,r3].
Sharp groin pain, sometimes with a click or catch, follows; the athlete may continue but symptoms recur with pivoting and deep flexion.
Loss of the seal lets cartilage consolidate faster under load, which may accelerate chondral damage over time [r3,r6].

variants.name: Degenerative / FAI-related
variants.description: Gradual onset in a hip with cam or pincer morphology. Cam causes chondrolabral separation; pincer crushes and degenerates the labrum.

variants.name: Dysplasia / instability
variants.description: Shallow socket; the labrum becomes hypertrophied and load-bearing and fails under repetitive overload. Often hypermobile women.

variants.name: Acute low-energy twist
variants.description: A pivot, slip or awkward landing in sport; about 30% of surgical cases report this onset [r5].

variants.name: High-energy trauma
variants.description: Hip subluxation or dislocation (e.g. a fall or tackle onto a flexed hip) tears the posterior or anterior labrum, often with chondral and capsular injury.

anatomy.text: The labrum is a triangular ring of fibrocartilage attached to the bony acetabular rim, continuous with the transverse acetabular ligament inferiorly. On its articular side it joins the hyaline cartilage through a narrow 1–2 mm transition zone; a projection of bone extends into its base via a zone of calcified cartilage [r2]. Blood supply enters from the capsular side, so the inner articular margin is relatively avascular. The labrum is innervated with free nerve endings and mechanoreceptors. Mechanically it deepens the socket and acts as a seal that pressurises the intra-articular fluid and slows cartilage consolidation [r3].

structures.name: Acetabular labrum
structures.role: Deepens the socket, seals the joint, pressurises synovial fluid and contributes to stability and proprioception [r3]

structures.name: Chondrolabral junction
structures.role: Transition between labral fibrocartilage and articular hyaline cartilage; the commonest tear site [r2]

structures.name: Acetabular articular cartilage
structures.role: Load-bearing surface that is protected by the labral seal; often damaged alongside the labrum [r6]

structures.name: Hip capsule (iliofemoral ligament)
structures.role: Restrains extension and external rotation; laxity increases labral load

structures.name: Gluteal muscles
structures.role: Hip extensors; strong gluteal contribution reduces anterior joint force in extension [r8]

structures.name: Iliopsoas
structures.role: Hip flexor and anterior dynamic stabiliser; reduced force increases anterior joint force in flexion [r8]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Two histological tear types occur. In the first, the labrum detaches from the articular cartilage at the transition zone. In the second, one or more cleavage planes split the labral substance. Both show new microvessel formation within the tear [r2]. Tears occur at the articular, not capsular, margin [r6]. Because the articular side is poorly vascularised, tears there have little capacity to heal spontaneously.

A torn labrum loses its sealing function. In cadaveric hips, removing the labrum reduced intra-articular fluid pressurisation and allowed the cartilage to consolidate about 21–22% faster under load [r3]. This is one explanation for the close association between labral and chondral damage: 73% of patients with labral fraying or tears had chondral change, supporting labral disruption and degenerative joint disease as part of one continuum [r6]. Pain arises from labral nerve endings, synovitis and associated cartilage and bone changes.

structures.name: Anterosuperior labrum
structures.effect: Chondrolabral detachment or intrasubstance cleavage tear [r2]

structures.name: Acetabular articular cartilage
structures.effect: Chondral softening, delamination or defects adjacent to the tear in most surgical cases [r6]

structures.name: Joint seal and synovial fluid
structures.effect: Reduced fluid pressurisation and faster cartilage consolidation under load [r3]

structures.name: Synovium
structures.effect: Reactive synovitis and small effusion after flares

structures.name: Capsule
structures.effect: Laxity (dysplasia, hypermobility) or stiffness (FAI) alters labral load

muscles.name: Gluteus maximus and medius
muscles.effect: Weakness or delayed recruitment increases anterior hip joint force during extension tasks [r8]

muscles.name: Iliopsoas
muscles.effect: Reduced force increases anterior joint force in flexion [r8]; it may also be guarded and tender, adding to anterior pain

muscles.name: Hip adductors and deep rotators
muscles.effect: Protective co-contraction and pain-related inhibition reduce dynamic control in single-leg tasks

cellular.description: Fibrocartilage collagen bundles separate at the chondrolabral junction. Bleeding is limited to the vascularised capsular margin.
Matrix fragments and cytokines inflame the synovium and sensitise labral free nerve endings.
New microvessels grow into the tear [r2]. Peripheral (capsular-side) tears may form fibrovascular scar; articular-side tears usually do not bridge.
Persisting instability of the torn fragment, mucoid change and calcification develop; adjacent cartilage softens and delaminates [r6].

systems.effect: Labral nociceptors and mechanoreceptors are disrupted. Pain sensitisation and altered proprioception contribute to apprehension and reduced single-leg control.
Synovitis drives flares, night pain and stiffness after loading (night pain was reported by 71% in one series) [r5].
Avoidance of hip extension and rotation shifts load to the lumbar spine, sacroiliac joint and pubic symphysis; a Trendelenburg gait was seen in 38% [r5].
Long diagnostic delay and multiple providers (mean 3.3 before diagnosis) can generate frustration, fear and catastrophising [r5].
Labral disruption and chondral change commonly coexist and may be early steps on the path to osteoarthritis [r6].

grades.description: The labrum separates from the articular cartilage at the transition zone [r2].
grades.prognosis: Typical of cam-type FAI; may be repairable arthroscopically

grades.description: One or more cleavage planes of variable depth within the labral substance [r2].
grades.prognosis: Typical of degenerative or pincer-related tears; often debrided rather than repaired

timeframes.summary: The articular side of the labrum has limited capacity to heal, so recovery reflects settling of synovitis and sensitisation and restoration of hip strength and control. Allow at least 3 months of exercise-based care before judging response [r11].

healing.description: Pain on rotation and loading; reduce provocative positions
Peripheral tears may scar; articular-side tears usually persist
Progressive hip and trunk strengthening and movement retraining
Repaired labrum heals back to the rim over about 3 months; follow the surgeon's protocol

milestones.label: Hip strength ≥80% of the other side
Return to running
milestones.note: Typical clinical range 10–16 weeks after repair

timeframes.returnToSport: Non-surgical: often 3–6 months with load modification. After arthroscopic labral repair: typically 4–9 months. Progression is criteria-based.

symptoms: Groin or anterior hip pain (92% in one series), sometimes buttock, lateral hip or thigh pain [r5]
Activity-related pain, especially with pivoting, deep flexion and prolonged sitting; night pain is common [r5]
Clicking, catching, locking or a sense of giving way
Stiffness and reduced tolerance of running, kicking or dance
Insidious onset in most; a specific twisting event in some [r5]
signs: Positive FADIR (impingement) test reproducing familiar groin pain (95% in one series) [r5]
Painful or apprehensive end-range flexion and internal rotation, or extension with external rotation
Limp or positive Trendelenburg sign in some patients [r5]
Reduced hip abductor and extensor strength
Painful click on moving the hip from flexion–abduction–external rotation into extension (anterior tears)

subjective: Mechanism: insidious versus twist, slip, fall or tackle; sport and positions that provoke pain
Mechanical symptoms: clicking, catching, locking, giving way, and the positions in which they occur
Symptoms of instability or hypermobility (dysplasia) versus stiffness (FAI)
Screen for serious pathology: night or rest pain unrelated to activity, fever, weight loss, history of cancer, bone stress risk factors [r1]
Previous diagnoses, treatments and providers (diagnosis is often delayed) [r5]
Goals, expectations and views on surgery
observation: Gait: antalgic or Trendelenburg pattern in some [r5]
Single-leg stance and squat: pelvic drop, femoral adduction
Posture: anterior pelvic tilt and hip extension habits in standing
palpation: Little focal tenderness; deep anterior hip pain is non-specific
Palpate iliopsoas, adductor origin and greater trochanter to identify competing pain sources
rangeOfMotion: Flexion and internal rotation at 90° flexion (restricted with FAI morphology)
Extension and external rotation (painful or apprehensive with anterior tears or instability)
Beighton score and hip external rotation range for hypermobility
strength: Hand-held dynamometry of hip abduction, extension, flexion, adduction and rotation; express as limb symmetry
functional: Deep squat, lunge and sport-specific pivot reproduction

specialTests.name: FADIR (flexion–adduction–internal rotation) test
specialTests.purpose: Screen for intra-articular pain including labral tear
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine. Flex the hip to 90°, then passively adduct and internally rotate it.
specialTests.sensitivity: Pooled 0.94 (95% CI 0.90–0.97) to 0.99 (95% CI 0.98–1.00) for FAI/labral tear

specialTests.name: Flexion–internal rotation test
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine. Flex the hip to 90° and apply internal rotation.

specialTests.name: Anterior apprehension (hyperextension–external rotation) test
specialTests.purpose: Anterior instability or anterior labral pathology
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine at the end of the couch or side-lying. Extend and externally rotate the hip.
specialTests.positive: Apprehension or reproduction of anterior groin pain.

specialTests.name: Resisted straight-leg raise (Stinchfield)
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine with the knee straight and the hip at 30° flexion. Resist hip flexion.

outcomeMeasures.name: iHOT-33 (International Hip Outcome Tool)
outcomeMeasures.use: Hip-related quality of life in young active adults; primary outcome in FASHIoN [r12]

outcomeMeasures.name: HAGOS (Copenhagen Hip and Groin Outcome Score)
outcomeMeasures.use: Symptoms, function and sport participation in athletes

imaging.modality: Plain radiographs (AP pelvis and lateral femoral head–neck view)
imaging.indication: First imaging to identify FAI morphology, dysplasia or osteoarthritis that underlie most tears [r1]
imaging.findings: Cam/pincer morphology, low lateral centre-edge angle (dysplasia), joint-space narrowing

imaging.indication: When the result will change management (e.g. surgical planning) or another diagnosis must be excluded
imaging.findings: Contrast or fluid tracking into the chondrolabral junction. Pooled sensitivity/specificity: MRI 0.80/0.77, MRA 0.89/0.69; 3 T MRI approaches MRA sensitivity [r10]. Tears are common in pain-free hips [r4].

imaging.indication: To confirm that pain is intra-articular before surgery
imaging.findings: Substantial short-term pain relief supports an intra-articular source

differentials.name: FAI syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Same symptoms plus cam or pincer morphology on radiographs and restricted flexion–internal rotation. Most labral tears coexist with FAI.

differentials.name: Iliopsoas-related groin pain
differentials.distinguishing: Pain with resisted hip flexion and iliopsoas stretch, with tenderness below the inguinal ligament.

differentials.name: Snapping hip syndrome (internal)
differentials.distinguishing: Audible, often visible snap as the hip moves from flexion–abduction–external rotation to extension; reproducible and usually painless or mildly painful.

differentials.name: Adductor-related groin pain
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness at the adductor longus origin and pain on resisted adduction.

differentials.name: Femoral neck stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Endurance or military training, pain on hopping and weight-bearing, night pain. MRI needed urgently.

differentials.name: Gluteal tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Lateral hip pain with tenderness at the greater trochanter and pain on single-leg stance; FADIR typically negative.

differentials.name: Lumbar referred pain
differentials.distinguishing: Spinal movement reproduces symptoms; neural tension or neurological signs.

redFlags: Constant, unremitting night or rest pain unrelated to activity, unexplained weight loss or history of cancer: suspect neoplasm. Arrange urgent medical review.
Groin pain with weight-bearing and hopping in a runner or recruit: exclude femoral neck stress fracture with urgent MRI before progressing load.
Fever with a hot, highly irritable hip and inability to weight-bear: suspect septic arthritis. Refer to emergency.
A truly locked hip that cannot be moved, or a hip that gave way with deformity after trauma: arrange urgent orthopaedic review.
After arthroscopy, calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness (VTE), wound infection or new numbness in the groin, thigh or foot (traction neuropraxia): arrange prompt medical review.

management.principles:
Confirm that the tear is the likely pain source using history, examination and imaging together, because labral tears are common in people without pain [r1,r4]. Address the underlying driver: FAI morphology, dysplasia or instability, and the loads that provoke symptoms. First-line care is education, activity modification and a progressive physiotherapist-led exercise program for at least 3 months, with physical activity maintained [r11]. Strengthening the gluteals and iliopsoas and avoiding sustained end-range hip extension may reduce anterior joint force [r8].

Arthroscopy (labral repair, refixation or debridement, plus treatment of FAI morphology) is considered when symptoms persist. Surgery produced greater improvement in hip-related quality of life than physiotherapist-led care in FAI syndrome trials in which labral tears were treated [r12,r14]. Where possible the labrum is repaired rather than resected to preserve the seal [r7,r13]. Rehabilitation after surgery is essential [r11].

medical.name: Hip arthroscopy: labral repair or refixation
medical.description: Reattachment of the labrum to the rim with suture anchors, usually with correction of FAI morphology. Compared with debridement, repair gave better pain, mHHS and satisfaction in pooled mainly observational studies [r13], and better 10-year joint survival in one study [r7].

medical.name: Hip arthroscopy versus physiotherapist-led care (FAI with labral pathology)
medical.description: In FASHIoN, arthroscopy improved iHOT-33 by 6.8 points more than personalised hip therapy at 12 months [r12]. In the Australian FASHIoN trial, iHOT-33 improved 14 points more after arthroscopy, but cartilage metabolism did not differ [r14].

medical.name: Labral debridement (partial resection)
medical.description: Removal of unstable, irreparable labral tissue. Short-term outcomes are acceptable, but loss of the seal may compromise long-term joint health [r3,r7].

medical.name: Image-guided intra-articular injection
medical.description: Anaesthetic (± corticosteroid) used mainly diagnostically; therapeutic effect is usually short-lived.

medical.name: Arthroscopy for an incidental tear or in established osteoarthritis
medical.description: Labral tears are common in pain-free hips [r4] and chondral change accompanies most tears [r6]; operating on an imaging finding without matching symptoms, or in a hip with established osteoarthritis, is not supported.

physio.name: Progressive exercise-based treatment for at least 3 months
physio.description: Individualised hip and trunk strengthening, neuromuscular control and functional retraining with education. Consensus recommends at least 3 months before judging response [r11].

physio.name: Gluteal and iliopsoas retraining with movement modification
physio.description: Train gluteal-led hip extension and iliopsoas-led flexion, and reduce habitual hip hyperextension in standing and gait, to lower anterior joint force [r8]. Based on modelling; clinical trials are lacking.

physio.name: Education and activity modification
physio.description: Explain that tears are common and not always painful [r4]; reduce provocative pivoting, end-range flexion–rotation and extension–external rotation loads while symptoms settle; keep active [r11].

physio.name: Post-operative rehabilitation
physio.description: Staged, physiotherapist-led rehabilitation after labral repair, respecting surgeon restrictions on weight-bearing, flexion, external rotation and extension [r11].

physio.name: Manual therapy
physio.description: May be used short term to ease pain and enable exercise. Not established as a stand-alone treatment [r11].

physio.name: Forced end-range stretching and repeated provocation of the click
physio.description: Repeatedly forcing the hip into painful end range or reproducing catching loads the torn labrum and usually aggravates synovitis.

education: Labral tears are very common, even in people with no hip pain. The scan is only one part of the picture.
The torn edge does not usually knit back together, but most people can calm the hip and regain function by strengthening and changing how they load it.
Avoid repeatedly pushing into the positions that click or catch while symptoms settle; keep moving within comfortable ranges.
Give a structured exercise program at least 3 months. Surgery is an option to discuss if symptoms persist.
If you have surgery, rehabilitation takes several months and protecting the repair early is important.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and guided by symptom response (pain ≤3/10 during exercise and settled within 24 hours) [r11]. Early work avoids end-range positions that load the torn labrum (deep flexion with internal rotation for anterosuperior FAI-related tears; extension with external rotation for anterior tears or instability). Gluteal-led extension and iliopsoas-led flexion are emphasised to reduce anterior joint force [r8]. After labral repair, follow the surgeon's protocol: typically protected weight-bearing for 2–6 weeks, flexion limited to about 90°, and no forced extension or external rotation for 3–6 weeks.

stages.name: Protect & settle
goals: Activate gluteals, iliopsoas and deep rotators in mid-range
precautions: Avoid pivoting on the affected leg and deep flexion with rotation
Avoid hip extension beyond neutral and external rotation stretches after repair

exercises.name: Isometric gluteal and abductor activation (supine or side-lying)
Double-leg glute bridge (partial range)
exercises.cues: Stop at neutral hip extension; feel the gluteals, not the back

exercises.name: Supine heel slide with iliopsoas activation
exercises.cues: Slide the heel up to about 70–90° hip flexion without groin pinch

exercises.name: Stationary cycling with a high seat
exercises.cues: Saddle high so the hip stays below 90°

progressionCriteria: Able to perform exercises without next-day flare
Surgeon clearance for full weight-bearing (if operated)

stages.name: Strength & control
goals: Build hip abductor, extensor, flexor and rotator strength
precautions: Introduce deeper flexion and rotation gradually
No impact or pivoting yet after repair
progressionCriteria: Single-leg squat without pelvic drop or valgus

stages.name: Load, power & running
goals: Return to running and linear acceleration
Tolerance of deeper flexion and rotation loads
precautions: Introduce pivoting and kicking in graded drills

exercises.name: Split squat progressing to Bulgarian split squat

progressionCriteria: No mechanical symptoms with sport-specific movements

stages.name: Return to sport
goals: Sport-specific pivoting, kicking, cutting or dance demands
Graded return to training and competition
precautions: Return to end-range sport positions (e.g. splits, deep goalkeeping) last

exercises.name: Strength maintenance (split squat, RDL, Copenhagen, bridges)

progressionCriteria: Acceptable HAGOS sport scores and athlete confidence

criteria: Pain ≤2/10 during and after full training, settling within 24 h
No locking or giving way during sport-specific tasks
Hip strength ≥90% limb symmetry for abduction, adduction, flexion and extension
Athlete confidence and acceptable patient-reported function
After repair: surgeon clearance and protocol completed
tests: Single, triple and side hop tests

prognosis: Many people improve with exercise-based care, but the torn articular labrum rarely heals. In surgical series 89% reported improvement at about 16 months after arthroscopy [r5]. In randomised trials of FAI syndrome, surgery including labral treatment gave modestly better patient-reported outcomes than physiotherapist-led care at 12 months [r12,r14]. Labral repair may preserve the joint better than resection: one study found 10-year survival of 78% after repair versus 46% after debridement [r7]. Labral and chondral damage commonly coexist and represent part of a degenerative continuum, so long-term osteoarthritis risk depends on hip morphology and cartilage status [r6].
prevention: No proven prevention exists. Maintaining hip strength, particularly gluteal and iliopsoas function, may reduce anterior joint loading [r8].
Manage the volume of repeated end-range flexion–rotation and extension–external rotation in training, especially in hips with FAI morphology or dysplasia.
clinicalPearls: A labral tear on MRI is common in pain-free hips (around 54%). Treat the patient, not the scan [r4].
Most tears are secondary. Look for FAI morphology, dysplasia or hypermobility on radiographs and examination, and treat the driver [r7].
Clicking is common in normal hips. A painful catch reproduced in a consistent position is more meaningful.
Patients often see several clinicians before diagnosis. Take groin pain with mechanical symptoms in a young adult seriously [r5].
Reduce anterior joint force: coach gluteal-led extension and limit habitual hip hyperextension in standing and gait [r8].
Hypermobile patients with labral tears need stability and control work, not stretching.

animation.title: How a hip labral tear happens

captions.text: A footballer sprints, then plants the right foot to change direction.
The right hip is flexed and loaded, with the foot fixed to the ground.
The pelvis and trunk twist over the planted femur, driving the head against the front of the socket.
Shear concentrates at the anterosuperior rim, where the labrum joins the cartilage.
A sharp groin pain and a click. Pivoting and deep flexion now reproduce it.
Zooming into the right hip from the front.

actions.text: Labrum: deepens and seals the socket

captions.text: The labrum is a fibrocartilage ring that deepens the socket and seals the joint fluid.
Rotation under load drives the femoral head against the anterosuperior labrum.
The labrum detaches from the cartilage at the chondrolabral junction.
Its nerve endings fire, producing deep groin pain and a catching sensation.
Synovitis and a small effusion follow.
With the seal lost, cartilage beside the tear is loaded harder and starts to soften.
The inner edge has little blood supply, so this tear rarely heals by itself.
Like the meniscus, the labrum is fibrocartilage: collagen bundles running around the rim.
Under rotational load, shear concentrates where the labrum meets the cartilage.
Collagen bundles separate: a tear on the articular side.
Near the capsule, vessels bring cells that can lay down scar.
On the avascular articular side, the tear stays open, so strength and load control matter.
